newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope says moral wilderness threatens Poland.
newsitem.headline: Pope says moral wilderness threatens Poland.

text.p: Pope John Paul told his Polish countrymen on Sunday that a moral wilderness threatened the freedom they won after decades of totalitarianism.
He also lashed out at criticism of the Roman Catholic Church, calling it Poland's true guardian of liberty.
On the second day of his trip home, the Pope further decried the scandal of "a geography of hunger", urging rich nations to put aside "unrestrained desire for profits" to help the poor.

The 77-year-old Pope, who has suffered from a series of health problems in recent years, appeared tired at the start of the mass before a crowd that police estimated at some 200,000 braving cold drizzle to see their most famous native son.
Vatican spokesman Joaquin Navarro-Valls said the Pope was "very well," adding: "One can see that he is happy to be home."
After a slow start, the Pope picked up steam in his sermon delivered from a carved wooden throne on an altar platform with a backdrop shaped like breaking waves.
He raised his voice almost to a shout, pulling no punches in comments applicable to Poland's political and social debate.
"True freedom demands order," he said. "We are talking first of all about the moral order, order in the sphere of values, the order of truth and goodness.

"When there is a void in the area of values -- when chaos and confusion reign in the moral sphere -- freedom dies, man is reduced from freedom to slavery, becoming a slave to passions, and pseudo-values," he said.
Since the fall of communism in 1989, the Pope has often expressed concern that Poland was losing part of its religious heritage as it eagerly embraced social and economic changes.
The Pope is visiting against the background of a domestic political battle centred in part around the role of the Church.

His seventh visit home comes in the midst of a campaign for a general election this year in which rightist opposition parties led by the pro-Catholic Solidarity union hope to supplant the secular-minded former communists now in government.
The Pope warned the crowd of the dangers of a society "permeated by ideas of democracy inspired by liberal ideology".

Last year the ex-communists linked with President Aleksander Kwasniewski and other liberal or leftist parties relaxed Poland's abortion law, a move which has just been challenged by a Polish Constitutional court.
Critics say the Church seeks too much influence. Leftists in parliament have stalled a Concordat treaty with the Vatican regulating such issues as religious education in schools.
Speaking like a stern schoolmaster to a people he considers his children, the Pope rejected accusations by some Poles that the powerful Roman Catholic Church was an obstacle to progress.

"Attempts are being made to convince man and whole societies that God is an obstacle on the path to full freedom, that the Church is an enemy of freedom, that she does not understand freedom, that she is afraid of it," he said, raising his voice.

"This is an unprecedented falsification of the truth," he said. "Saying that the Church is an enemy of freedom makes no sense, especially here in Poland. The Church has proved many times in the last 50 years that it is the guardian of freedom."
The Pope said freedom in Poland and other Eastern European countries "makes the heart beat faster" because it was so hard-won after decades of Nazi and Communist totalitarianism.

"Deep are the wounds that remain from that in the human spirit from that period. Much time must yet pass before they will be completely healed," said the Pope, who had earlier called for reconciliation in Polish society.
Security at the ceremony was very tight, with even priests and nuns going through metal detectors and being frisked.
The Pope's words struck a chord among the crowd, many of whom had waited in the rain through the night to see him.
"It is unjust that people who tried to suppress the Church in Poland are now in power," said Jolanta Wilkonska, a woman in her 50s who came from Warsaw for the occasion.
In another part of his homily, the Pope repeated the thrust of his November address to the U.N. World Food Summit in Rome.
"At this moment millions of our brothers and sisters are suffering from hunger and many are dying of it," he said.

"The earth is capable of feeding everyone...we must finally put an end to the scourge of hunger. May solidarity prevail over the unrestrained desire for profit and way of applying trade laws which do not take into account inalienable human beings."
